## Where we are

| Model | Determinism | Time | State | Representation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ODE, function map | deterministic | cont. or discrete | continuous | population |
| Markov chain | stochastic | discrete | discrete | population |
| Jump process | stochastic | continuous | discrete | population |
| SDE | stochastic | continuous | continuous | population |
| **Agent-based (next)** | **stochastic** | **discrete** | **discrete** | **individual** |

Sensitivity, identifiability, and observation models are questions asked *about*
any of these. Today asks what to *do* with one.

::: {.notes}
The Day 3 recap slot. Everything so far has been a population model, where the
state is counts; the final session fills the individual column, where the state
is people. This session moves along a different axis again: not a new model
class, but a decision made with a model you already have.
:::

## What this session is for

- A tour of what specialised packages add **once a model exists**.
- The scenario half is machinery you already have: the Day 1 lockdown callback,
  reused. A vaccination campaign is the same pattern on a different parameter.
- The optimisation half works one small problem end to end, so the *shape* of an
  optimisation is recognisable when you meet a bigger one.
- You leave with pointers, not with a complete treatment of optimal control.

::: {.notes}
Say this out loud at the start. The aim is recognition and orientation, not
mastery: nobody should feel they are behind because they cannot yet write an
optimal-control problem from scratch. Everything in the first half is a callback
they have already used; everything in the second half is one worked example plus
a reading list.
:::

## Scenario first, optimization second

An intervention analysis has two auditable layers:

1. specify a policy and simulate it;
2. compare admissible policies with an explicit objective and constraints.

The baseline is the course SIR model. A 50% transmission reduction lasts
$d=10$ time units; only its start $t_1\in[0,25]$ is optimized.

::: {.notes}
Separating these layers prevents an optimizer from hiding an implementation
error or an implicit policy assumption.
:::

## Controlled SIR equations

Add cumulative incidence $C$ and a rectangular control:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot S&=-\beta c(1-v(t))SI/N,\\
\dot I&=\beta c(1-v(t))SI/N-\gamma I,\\
\dot R&=\gamma I,\\
\dot C&=\beta c(1-v(t))SI/N,
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
v(t;t_1)=
\begin{cases}
v_{\max},&t_1\le t<t_1+d,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

The teaching objective is $J(t_1)=C(T;t_1)$ at $T=45$.

::: {.notes}
This is a deterministic, continuous-time, continuous-state, population model.
The control is a population-level coefficient, not an individual simulation.
:::

## A callback defines one policy

```{julia}
#| label: fig-slide-ch11-scenario
#| fig-cap: "A callback-defined policy compared with no intervention."
using CairoMakie
using DiffEqCallbacks
using OrdinaryDiffEq

β11, c11, γ11, N11 = 0.05, 10.0, 0.25, 1000.0
u011 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0]
function policy11!(du, u, p, t)
    β, c, γ, reduction, N = p
    incidence = β * c * (1 - reduction) * u[1] * u[2] / N
    du[1], du[2], du[3], du[4] = -incidence, incidence - γ*u[2],
        γ*u[2], incidence
end
grid11 = collect(0.0:0.5:45.0)
function scenario11(start; duration = 10.0, reduction = 0.5)
    p = [β11, c11, γ11, 0.0, N11]
    stop = start + duration
    affect!(integrator) = (integrator.p[4] =
        integrator.t < stop ? reduction : 0.0)
    cb = PresetTimeCallback([start, stop], affect!)
    solve(ODEProblem(policy11!, u011, (0.0, 45.0), p), Tsit5();
        callback = cb, saveat = grid11, abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8)
end
none11 = solve(ODEProblem(policy11!, u011, (0.0, 45.0),
    [β11, c11, γ11, 0.0, N11]), Tsit5(); saveat = grid11)
policy11 = scenario11(8.0)
a11, b11 = Array(none11), Array(policy11)
fig11 = Figure(size = (820, 600))
ax11a = Axis(fig11[1, 1], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "infectious")
lines!(ax11a, grid11, a11[2, :], label = "none")
lines!(ax11a, policy11.t, b11[2, :], label = "50% reduction")
vspan!(ax11a, 8.0, 18.0, color = (:steelblue, 0.15))
axislegend(ax11a)
ax11b = Axis(fig11[2, 1], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "cumulative incidence")
lines!(ax11b, grid11, a11[4, :], label = "none")
lines!(ax11b, policy11.t, b11[4, :], label = "policy")
vspan!(ax11b, 8.0, 18.0, color = (:steelblue, 0.15))
fig11
```

::: {.notes}
`PresetTimeCallback` changes the parameter at two known times. It implements
the scenario; it does not search over policies.
:::

## Bounded timing optimization

Four pieces: objective, derivative rule, starting point and box, method.

```{julia}
#| label: ch11-slide-optimize
using Optimization
using OptimizationOptimJL

final_incidence11(x, _) = Array(scenario11(x[1]))[4, end]

objective11 = OptimizationFunction(final_incidence11, AutoFiniteDiff())
problem11 = OptimizationProblem(objective11, [8.0], nothing;
    lb = [0.0], ub = [25.0])
solution11 = solve(problem11, Fminbox(LBFGS()); maxiters = 30)
optimal11 = solution11.u[1]
```

::: {.notes}
Read the four pieces aloud in order rather than explaining the algorithm. The
finite-difference rule is chosen because each objective evaluation runs a whole
ODE solve. `solve` is the same verb as for an ODEProblem: a different problem
type selects a different method.
:::

## The grid confirms the optimizer

```{julia}
#| label: fig-slide-ch11-objective
#| fig-cap: "Final cumulative incidence across admissible intervention starts, with the optimizer's answer marked."
starts11 = collect(0.0:1.0:25.0)
values11 = [Array(scenario11(t))[4, end] for t in starts11]
fig11o = Figure(size = (780, 400))
ax11o = Axis(fig11o[1, 1], xlabel = "start time", ylabel = "C(45)")
lines!(ax11o, starts11, values11, color = :darkorange)
scatter!(ax11o, [starts11[argmin(values11)]],
    [minimum(values11)], color = :grey, markersize = 12,
    label = "grid diagnostic")
scatter!(ax11o, [optimal11], [final_incidence11([optimal11], nothing)],
    color = :firebrick, markersize = 14, label = "optimizer")
axislegend(ax11o)
fig11o
```

::: {.notes}
The optimizer returns a continuous timing estimate; the grid shows whether the
objective is flat or has several plausible starts. Both are computed here, so
the two markers agreeing is the check.
:::

## Validation, interpretation, and limits

For every solved policy check

$$
\max_t|S(t)+I(t)+R(t)-N|<10^{-6},\qquad
\Delta C(t)\ge 0.
$$

- The “optimal” result is conditional on reduction, duration, horizon, and cost.
- Instantaneous switching, perfect adherence, homogeneous mixing, and a closed population are idealizations.
- Add intervention cost, capacity, equity, uncertainty, or a peak-infection penalty when those are decision requirements.
